newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany may raise VAT in tax reform-sources.
newsitem.headline: Germany may raise VAT in tax reform-sources.

text.p: Germany could raise value-added tax by one percentage point to help finance big income tax cuts planned for 1999, sources in Finance Minister Theo Waigel's coalition tax working group said on Monday.
The working group agreed on the VAT hike but the move still has to go through a long process involving the three German coalition parties if it is to be incorporated into a major tax reform package.
Waigel wants the net load on German taxpayers to be lightened by about 30 billion marks ($19 billion) to help boost jobs and investment in the country's struggling economy.
This involves a juggling act under which he would make 70 billion marks in tax cuts but also raise new revenue covering part of the amount.
The VAT increase would raise 15 billion marks, added to a further 33 billion in extra revenues to be raised from scrapping tax breaks, the sources said.
Final decisions on the tax reform package are planned to be made at a meeting on January 22, ushering in a consultative political process which Chancellor Helmut Kohl has said could take all year.
However, the tax commission, meeting for the penultimate time before it is due to complete its reform proposals next week, failed to agree on new income tax rates.
Waigel said after the meeting that two income tax proposals were still being discussed -- sticking to the current sliding scale or creating a stepped system of three tax brackets.

The entry tax rate was likely to be 20 percent or below, down from the current 26 percent. But Waigel did not say what the top rate, currently 53 percent, would be. He has said in the past the top rate would fall below 40 percent.

Both Waigel, who favours the linear system, and leaders from junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP), who back a simpler three-tier concept, said the financial impact of their income tax proposals would be similar.

Waigel said that the question of taxing pensions had still not yet been decided, and would be addressed at a joint meeting of the tax panel and a pensions reform working group headed by Social Security Minister Norbert Bluem.
